Add documents Leverage RAG What Autopilot reads The documents you select, in full Only the relevant passages from a search index your admin set up (Context Grounding) Best for Requirements whose rules live in a few known documents Requirements with terms or abbreviations whose meaning is spread across many sources

    In this workshop, use Add documents. RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) means Autopilot first looks up the relevant passages, then writes.

  4. On the next screen:

    1. Select a prompt: choose Valid E2E Scenario Testing.

      Editing prompts and adding your own

      ✅ For this run only – edit the prompt right here.

      ✅ For the whole project – create new prompts or edit existing ones in the Prompt Library, under Project Settings.

    2. At the end of the prompt text, on a new line, add these instructions:

      Generate 5 test cases. Give every step one action and an expected result, and add preconditions and postconditions. Name every UI element exactly as it is labelled in UiBank. Start steps with Select, Type, Get Text, Check or Select item. Include 1 test case for an applicant aged 66, with a loan amount of 50000, a term of 3 years and a yearly income of 90000, that expects the loan to be rejected, and name it Submit Over-65 Request.

      Why "Select, Type, Get Text…"? Steps written as one clear action each are easier for everyone who runs them later today: you, Delegate and a robot.

    3. Keep the default model.

    4. Select Generate tests. Autopilot takes about a minute. You can close the panel while it works.

  5. Under Latest activity, select Generated test cases to see the proposals.

See Generate tests for requirement.

docs.title: Review and keep the best
docs.text:
Autopilot drafts; you approve. Treat each proposal like a test case from a new team member.

  1. Expand each proposal and keep it only if it:

    ✅ traces to one acceptance criterion of Submit Loan Request

    ✅ has one action per step, each with an expected result

    ✅ uses realistic data (an email, an amount, a term, an income, an age)

    ✅ expects what the requirement says – not what you guess UiBank does

    Otherwise sharpen the instructions and generate again.

    Check approvals over $100,000

    The requirement says loans over $100,000 are approved when the income is more than 3x the amount – but UiBank never approves a loan over $100,000. A proposal that expects such an approval would fail as a second UiBank defect. That's a real finding, but not today's story: leave it out.

  2. Tick at least 3 proposals, including the over-65 one. When you tick the first box, a line N selected / Deselect all appears above the list and pushes it down. Check that your ticks are on the right rows, then select Create tests. With more proposals, the list can span more than one page.

    The message Test cases created and linked to the requirement. confirms it.

    In production, a second reviewer can sign off generated test cases with Testing Process Governance – you'll see it as an option in step 9.

  3. Open the requirement's Test Cases tab. Your new test cases are listed there: Autopilot links them to Submit Loan Request for you.

docs.title: Name your over-65 test case
docs.text:
One of your new test cases submits a loan request for an applicant over 65 – for example age 66 – and expects it to be rejected. It's the test case that decides the release, and steps 4, 6, 7 and 9 look for it by name.

  1. Find it on the requirement's Test Cases tab.
  2. Check its name. If it isn't exactly Submit Over-65 Request, open the test case and rename it to Submit Over-65 Request.
  3. Open its manual steps. The age step uses an age over 65 (66–70), and the last expected result is a rejection – not "Congrats! You've been approved…".
  4. Check that it uses amount 50000, term 3 and income 90000 – the same data as the trainer's automated test. With an amount over $100,000, UiBank rejects the loan for the amount, and you won't see the age defect. Edit the steps if needed.

No over-65 test case?

Generate again with only this instruction, or create it yourself: Test Cases → create a test case named Submit Over-65 Request, link it to Submit Loan Request, and add the steps of a loan application with amount 50000, term 3, income 90000 and age 66 that expects a rejection. Ask your trainer if you're stuck – you need this test case for the rest of the day.

Check it

✅ At least 3 new test cases are linked to Submit Loan Request (its Test Cases tab shows 9 or more).

✅ One of them is named Submit Over-65 Request, uses an age over 65, and expects a rejection.

✅ Each new test case has manual steps with an expected result.

docs.title: Bring your own sources (optional)
docs.text:
Your team rarely starts from a blank page. Try one of these if you finish early.

Bring your Excel UAT scripts (about 10 minutes)

Many teams keep UAT scripts in spreadsheets. Autopilot can turn them into manual test cases.

  1. Download UiBank Regression Tests.xlsx. It's also in your project, under Dashboard → Attachments.
  2. Go to Test Cases → Import Test Cases ▾ → Start new import.
  3. Under Provide import document, select Add a file, pick the .xlsx, then Next.
  4. Under Provide import instructions, type Import all the manual test cases., keep the recommended Model, and select Preview import.
  5. Autopilot says "Generating import preview, hold on" and that you can close the panel. It takes about 5 minutes – carry on with something else.
  6. Go back to Import Test Cases ▾ → Refine last import. When it's ready, you see Review import candidates.

  7. Tick the candidates you want – the spreadsheet holds an over-65 script (age 66, expects a rejection) – and select Create tests.

    Rows with the same test case name in one sheet are dropped without a warning – give each script a unique name.

The message "Test cases created." confirms it. Imported test cases aren't linked to a requirement: link the ones you keep from Submit Loan Request → Assign test case.

See Import manual test cases.

From a business document, with Delegate (about 10 minutes)

The business has documented a new process, Loan lookup, in a Process Design Document (PDD). It isn't in your requirements yet. Delegate, the desktop agent you connected in Prerequisites, can turn it into a requirement and a test case. On a Mac, Delegate for macOS (Preview) runs the same prompt.

  1. Download the PDD, Loan lookup process to be tested.docx.

  2. Attach it in Delegate. Replace <PROJECT_PREFIX> with your project prefix from step 1 (for example UIBAS), then paste:

    Analyze the attached PDD and create + save a requirement and a manual test case in my Test Manager project <PROJECT_PREFIX>.

Requirement: Create one new requirement for the process described in the PDD (don't create it if an existing requirement already covers this exact process – check first and tell me if you find one instead of creating a duplicate). Name it Loan Lookup. Its description should summarize the user flow (pages/actions) and any acceptance criteria from the PDD.
Test case: Create one manual test case - infer name from the PDD, derived from the PDD's numbered steps/screenshots – one test step per documented UI action, each with an expected result. Don't use the loan ID shown in the PDD: the step that enters the loan ID should use a loan ID from a loan applied for today.
Final step: After the PDD's last action, add a step that verifies the loan details page shows the same loan ID that was entered, along with the rest of the loan's details.
Link: Link the new test case to the new requirement.
Report back: give me the created requirement key and test case key when done.

  3. Approve Delegate's actions when it asks. It reports the new requirement key and test case key.

Check it

A new Loan Lookup requirement in your project, with a linked test case that has manual steps.

Not quite right? Talk to Delegate. Open the new requirement and test case in Test Manager. Check the title, description, acceptance criteria, steps and expected results. Then tell Delegate what to fix, in your own words, as you'd tell a colleague. For example:

✅ "The test case must check that the loan ID is the same, and that the loan's other details are displayed"

✅ "Don't use the data from the PDD in the test case"

✅ "Add the label 'Delegate' to this test case and requirement"

Want to run it too? Paste:

Apply for a loan in UiBank at https://uibank.uipath.com, note the new loan ID it shows, then run the new Loan Lookup test case with that loan ID.

UiBank's button for Loan Lookup is Already Have A Loan?. The loan details page always shows a sample email address – that's not a defect. UiBank may drop old loans, so apply for a new one if you rerun on another day.

docs.title: Nice work!
docs.text:
You've gone from a requirement to reviewed, traceable test cases in minutes – and Submit Over-65 Request is ready for its first run.

Next → 4. Run the Test Three Ways

docs.title: 4. Run the Test Three Ways
docs.text:
Leads: UAT · Tools: Test Manager Robot Delegate

Start the robot first Run it yourself Hand it to Delegate Check your three runs

Why it matters for you: UAT sign-off needs evidence. Here you see what a person, a desktop agent and a robot each record for the same test case, and whether all three catch the same UiBank defect.

You run Submit Over-65 Request, the test case you made in 3. Generate Test Cases, three times: on a robot, yourself, and with Delegate.

UiBank has a defect. An applicant aged 66 gets Congrats! You've been approved…, but the requirement says applicants over 65 must be rejected. So a correct run of this test case fails. That's the result you're looking for.

Start the robot first

The robot is shared by the whole class and runs one test at a time. Start your robot run before anything else on this page. Its result comes in after lunch.

docs.title: Three testers, one test case
docs.text: Who does the steps Where Evidence it leaves What it uses Your time Run autonomously (Preview) Autopilot, on the trainer's shared robot A cloud machine A result for each step, screenshots, comments it writes itself, Autopilot's reasoning App Test Platform Units, from the tenant ~3 min to start You (Execute Manually) You Your browser Pass or fail for each step, your comments, your screenshots Your time only ~10 min Delegate Delegate, the desktop agent Your browser, with your mouse and keyboard A result for each step, a trace for each step, a final screenshot Your AI usage allowance ~10 min

docs.title: 1 – Start the robot first (Preview)
docs.text:
Run autonomously (Autonomous Test Execution) gives one manual test case to Autopilot. Autopilot reads the steps and does them in a browser on a robot, with no automation built.

Preview

Labels and behavior may change. Your tenant may show slightly different labels.

  1. Go to Test Cases. On the Submit Over-65 Request row, select ⋮ → Execute Autonomously. Or open the test case and select Execute ▾ → Autonomously.

    You can also open the test case, go to the Manual Steps tab and select Run Autonomously in the right-hand panel:

  2. The Run test autonomously (Preview) panel opens. Its banner says the feature is only for web-based UI tests. That's fine: UiBank is a web app.

  3. On the first screen:

    ✅ Url: https://uibank.uipath.com, the UiBank home page. Your generated test case starts on the home page, so don't use the loan form's address. You can't go on without it.

    • Field empty? Type https://uibank.uipath.com.
    • Field already filled? Check that it shows exactly https://uibank.uipath.com. If not, clear the field first (select all, then delete), then type it. Typing into a filled field adds your text to the old address, and the run fails.

    The Url you type here is saved into the test case's Manual Steps → URL field and pre-filled next time. You can also set it once there.

    ✅ Model: keep the one marked Recommended.

    ✅ Enable live streaming: leave it off. Your trainer streams one run for the whole class.

    Select Next.

  4. On the second screen:

    ✅ Select folder: leave it as it is. It shows your project's Default Folder from step 1, ATB - Agentic Testing Workshop.

    ✅ Runtime type – the kind of robot machine that does the run. Your trainer tells you which one to use. On the workshop tenant it's Cloud - VM Testing, the trainer's shared cloud machine, usually already selected. Don't pick a Serverless runtime: the list shows them, but Run autonomously doesn't support them.

    ✅ Robot account: Any User/Robot account.

    ✅ Machine template: Any machine template.

    Select Run – once only. Every extra click adds another run to the shared queue. Wait for the panel's progress messages instead of clicking again.

  5. The panel shows its progress and ends with Autonomous test execution job triggered. You can close the panel now.

    In Execution, the run is named Submit Over-65 Request - followed by the date and time, and its type is Autonomous.

Waiting is normal

The shared robot runs one test at a time, about 6 minutes each. The first run of the day can also wait several minutes while the cloud machine starts. With the whole class in the queue, your run may finish only after lunch. Leave it and carry on: you read its result in 5. Compare the Runs.

If the panel shows an error, tell your trainer.

A run that ends after about a minute, with step 1 Failed, didn't reach the age decision – it's not a UiBank defect. Check the test case's Manual Steps → URL field for a broken address and fix it. If Behaviour verification on step 1 says "Verification could not be completed (HttpRequestException)", it was a service error. Either way, ask your trainer before you start another run – each run costs App Test Platform Units – and use the trainer's completed run in step 5.

Run autonomously uses App Test Platform Units from the tenant, not your personal AI allowance. See Running Autonomous Test Execution.

docs.title: 2 – Run it yourself
docs.text:
You run the steps in UiBank and record each result in the manual execution assistant, Test Manager's window for manual runs. This is the core UAT skill: a person checks the app and leaves evidence.

  1. Go to Test Cases and open Submit Over-65 Request. Select Execute ▾ → Manually (Test Cloud only).

    You can also select ⋮ → Execute Manually on its row in Test Cases. The list sorts by Last Modified, so the row can move: check the name before you click.

    This starts a run of this one test case, with no test set.

    No Execute Manually, or the window misbehaves?

    Create a test set with only Submit Over-65 Request, then on the set select Execute → Manually.

    Allow pop-ups for Test Manager

    The manual execution assistant opens in a new window. If nothing opens, allow pop-ups for Test Manager in your browser, then select Execute Manually again.

  2. Open UiBank in another window, next to the assistant.

  3. If the test case has a precondition, the state the app must be in before the test, set up UiBank as it says.
  4. Do each step in UiBank, then select Set Passed or Set Failed in the assistant. To pass several steps in a row, select Set Passed Till Here.

  5. At the step that checks the decision, UiBank shows Congrats! You've been approved… for your 66-year-old applicant. Your test case expects a rejection. Select Set Failed and add a comment, for example:

    UiBank approved a 66-year-old applicant. The requirement says applicants over 65 must be rejected.

  6. Add evidence to the failed step: a screenshot of UiBank's approval page. Open the step's ⋮ menu and select Capture screen, or Upload attachment for a file. Add image from clipboard stays greyed out until you copy an image. The attachment shows as an image icon under your comment.

    Capture doesn't work?

    Take a screenshot with your computer's own tool and select Upload attachment. If you can't attach a file either, describe what you saw in the comment. If capturing switches you to another tab, switch back to the assistant yourself.

  7. The postcondition box has a Condition met checkbox, ticked by default. The postcondition says the loan is rejected, but UiBank approved it: untick Condition met. Then select Done. There's no Next: the window closes by itself.

    Always finish with Done

    If you close the window without Done, the run stays Running in Execution.

Made a mistake?

A run started without a test set can't be run again. Start a new Execute Manually instead. See Executing test cases without a test set.

docs.title: 3 – Hand it to Delegate
docs.text:
Delegate, the desktop agent, runs the same steps in your browser with your mouse and keyboard. It then records the result in Test Manager. You watch, answer its questions and approve what it saves.

Use the QA / Testing session you set up in Prerequisites. Delegate is generally available on Windows. On a Mac, Delegate for macOS (Preview) runs the same prompts.

No Delegate?

Skip this part and pair with a neighbour: watch their Delegate run. Your robot run and your own run are enough for 5. Compare the Runs.

It's your turn now!

  1. Keep only one UiBank tab open. Delegate finds the window by its title, and the prompt names UiBank.
  2. Before your first prompt, attach only the browser window with UiBank to the chat (the screen icon next to the chat box). Delegate then sees nothing else on your screen.

  3. Find two values in Test Manager:

    ✅ <PROJECT_PREFIX>: your project's prefix, which you typed when you imported the project in step 1.

    ✅ <TEST_CASE_KEY>: the key of Submit Over-65 Request, in the Key column of Test Cases. A key is your prefix, a colon and a number.

  4. Replace both placeholders, then paste:

    In Test Manager project <PROJECT_PREFIX>, run the manual test case <TEST_CASE_KEY> (Submit Over-65 Request). Open UiBank at https://uibank.uipath.com, follow the test case's manual steps in the browser, and check every expected result. Stop and ask me if a step is unclear. Take a screenshot of the final result page and save it to my Desktop. When you finish, push the results to Test Manager, give me the link to the execution, and explain the reason for any failed step.

    It takes about 10 minutes. Delegate uses your mouse and keyboard, so don't touch them until it reports back. Follow its progress in the task list. If your screen locks, unlock it, and Delegate carries on.

  5. If Delegate asks you something, answer in plain words, as you would a colleague. For example: "The field is labelled Age. Type 66 there."

  6. When Delegate asks for permission to push the results to Test Manager, approve it. Read every other request before you approve it, too.
  7. Read its explanation of the failure. Does it call it a defect in UiBank or a problem with the test case?

Delegate says it can't reach Test Manager?

Your one-time connection from Prerequisites has probably expired. Repeat the sign-in in Connect Delegate to Test Manager, then paste the prompt again.

Delegate keeps retrying the failing step?

Tell it: "Mark this step Failed with what you see on the screen, and carry on." Still stuck? Run Submit Standard Loan Request with Delegate instead. It passes, but you still see how Delegate records a run. In the checks below and in step 5, your Delegate run is then Passed on Submit Standard Loan Request – that's expected, and the defect evidence comes from your own run and the robot's.

Think about it

Did Delegate stop to ask about a step, or do something you didn't expect? The same steps feed Run autonomously now, and the automation in 6. Automate with Studio Web. An unclear step costs time for every tester, person or agent.

Note the step. Don't change it yet: your robot run is still waiting and uses the same steps. You fix it in 5. Compare the Runs.

Beyond running tests – Delegate across the whole manual testing cycle

Ideas to try on your own project, in your own words:

✅ Find test ideas – from a requirement's acceptance criteria, or from a screenshot of a screen, including boundary and negative cases.

✅ Write the steps – turn those ideas into manual test cases and link them to the requirement.

✅ Run them with you – Delegate runs the steps and stops to ask when it needs a decision from you. Never paste passwords into the chat.

✅ Record the results – create test results with screenshots of failed steps, and upload them to Test Manager.

See Manual test execution with Delegate.

docs.title: Check your three runs
docs.text:
Check it

Go to Execution:

✅ Your own run of Submit Over-65 Request shows Failed, with your comment and your screenshot (or description) on the decision step.

✅ The Delegate run shows Failed, with a result for each step and a Delegate trace attached to the steps. Delegate names it Delegate- followed by the test case name and the date. The final screenshot is on your Desktop.

✅ Your robot run is listed as Submit Over-65 Request - followed by the date and time, with the type Autonomous. It's fine if it hasn't finished yet. Can't find it? Ask your trainer, who can see the queue.

docs.title: Nice work!
docs.text:
You ran the same test case as a tester, with Delegate, and on a robot. Both finished runs caught UiBank's over-65 defect. After lunch, you compare all three.

Next → 5. Compare the Runs

docs.title: 5. Compare the Runs
docs.text:
Leads: UAT · Tools: Test Manager Robot Trainer

Read the robot's run Compare the three runs Make one step agent-proof Watch Autonomous Exploration

Why it matters for you: AI testers leave a lot of evidence, but you still decide whether to trust it. Reading the three runs side by side shows you what a good step looks like: one that a colleague, Delegate and a robot all follow the same way.

Over lunch, the shared robot worked through the queue. Now you read what Autopilot did with your Submit Over-65 Request test case and compare it with your own run and Delegate's.

docs.title: Read the robot's run
docs.text:
1. Go to Execution and open the run of Submit Over-65 Request that you started with Run autonomously in step 4.

    The robot's run shows the type Autonomous, and its name is Submit Over-65 Request - followed by the date and time. Skip the run whose name starts with Delegate- and the one with your own comment. The robot's run has a Tester comment that Autopilot wrote and a screenshot under every step.

    Not finished yet?

    If your run is still waiting or running, don't start another one. Your trainer has a completed robot run of Submit Over-65 Request in the trainer's demo project: read that one instead, on your screen or on the projector. Come back to yours at the end of the day.

    If your run ended with an error before it reached the age decision, the problem is the robot or the service, not UiBank. A typical sign: the run took about a minute, step 1 is Failed, the other steps show None, and expanding step 1 may show "Verification could not be completed (HttpRequestException)" under Behaviour verification. Check the test case's Manual Steps → URL field for a broken address (it must be exactly https://uibank.uipath.com) and fix it. Ask your trainer before you start another run – each run costs App Test Platform Units – and use the trainer's run.

  2. The result page has the tabs Logs, Robot Logs, Execution details and Affected requirements. On the Logs tab, each step shows its result, the description and expected behaviour from your test case, a Tester comment that Autopilot wrote, and an attachment.

  3. Expand a step (Show execution trace):

    ✅ Sub-steps – what Autopilot did in the browser, with a screenshot of each action. You can zoom in or download it.

    ✅ Behaviour verification – how Autopilot checked the expected behaviour, and what it found.

  4. Open the Robot Logs tab. This is the execution log, with the columns Level, Time, Message and Info. It first lists the setup (package, process, robot), then Autopilot's reasoning for each step – how it found a field, what it typed, and how it compared the result with what you expected. The robot works in Microsoft Edge.

  5. Find the age decision step. It's Failed: Autopilot's comment reads like The result page displays the decision message: Congrats! You've been approved for a loan with UiBank!, and the screenshot shows the approval page – where your test case expects a rejection. If the run stopped before it, read the trainer's run instead (see the box above).

Preview

Run autonomously is a Preview feature. Labels and behavior may change. Your tenant may show slightly different labels.

See Reviewing Autonomous Test Execution results.

docs.title: Compare the three runs
docs.text:
Copy this table into your notes and fill in the last row. The other rows are already filled in for you.

You (Execute Manually) Delegate Robot (Run autonomously) Who did the steps You, in your browser Delegate, on your computer Autopilot, on the trainer's shared robot Evidence Pass or fail per step, your comment, your screenshot Result per step, a trace per step, a final screenshot Result per step, screenshots of every action, its own comments, its reasoning Time About 10 minutes of your time About 10 minutes, with your computer busy About 6 minutes on the robot, plus the wait in the queue Cost Your time Your AI usage allowance App Test Platform Units, from the tenant Result at the age decision Failed Failed Failed Where it hesitated or stumbled your notes your notes your notes

The table's main point: the same test case gave the same verdict three times. The defect is in UiBank, not in the tester.

Robot runs have their own type in reports

A run started with Run autonomously shows the type Autonomous, not Manual. Keep this in mind in 8. Read the Results: autonomous runs are counted separately from people's manual runs.

Cost details: Delegate and Autopilot chat use your monthly AI usage allowance, see Autopilot usage pool for testing. Run autonomously uses the tenant's App Test Platform Units, see Autonomous Test Execution.

docs.title: Make one step agent-proof
docs.text:
A person fills gaps from experience. An agent follows the words. Look at your notes and the robot's reasoning, and find one step that made Delegate or Autopilot hesitate, or that could be read two ways.

These patterns usually cause trouble:

Unclear step Why an agent struggles Better Enter the applicant's details and submit Several actions in one step; no data Type 66 in the Age field (one action per step) Click the button Which button? Select Submit (the label exactly as UiBank shows it) Check the result No expected result to compare with Expected behaviour: The page shows "Sorry, at this time you have not been approved for a loan."
  1. Open Submit Over-65 Request → Manual Steps.
  2. Rewrite the step you picked: one action, the UI label exactly as UiBank shows it, and an expected result with exact text. Changes save automatically.
Prefer to ask Delegate?

Replace the placeholders as in step 4, then paste:

Rewrite the steps of test case <TEST_CASE_KEY> in Test Manager project <PROJECT_PREFIX> that were unclear during this run, so each one has a single clear action and expected result. Show me the changes before you save them to Test Manager.

Keep the expected rejection

Don't change what the test case expects at the age decision. The requirement says over-65 applicants must be rejected. If you change the expected result to match UiBank, the test stops catching the defect.

docs.title: Watch: Autonomous Exploration (Preview)
docs.text:
Trainer

Autonomous Exploration doesn't need a test case. You give Autopilot a requirement, a web address and a time limit. It learns the app, plans test scenarios, runs as many as it can and reports what it found. Your trainer shows it, because it runs on the same shared robot.

Preview

Autonomous Exploration is a Preview feature, on Windows robots only. Labels and behavior may change. Your tenant may show slightly different labels.

What the trainer does:

  1. Opens the Submit Loan Request requirement and selects + Autonomous Exploration.

  2. In the Autonomous Exploration (Preview) panel, fills in:

    ✅ Instructions for Autopilot (optional), typed or picked with Prompt. A narrow one works best, for example "Only test the over-65 age rule."

    ✅ Test URL, the UiBank address.

    ✅ Timebox (minutes), for example 10.

    ✅ Model, and Enable live streaming so the class can watch.

  3. Selects Next, checks Select folder, Runtime type, Robot account and Machine template as in step 4, and selects Start Autonomous Exploration.

  4. While it runs, the trainer can pause and guide Autopilot with a typed hint.
  5. Then the trainer opens a run made earlier, because 10 minutes covers only about one scenario. The report has three tabs: Scenarios, Robot logs and Documents.

What you look for in the report:

✅ How many scenarios Autopilot planned, and how many it completed. In one 10-minute run before the workshop, it planned 13 scenarios and completed one: an under-18 rejection, with a finding about the age message.

✅ Each finding's category (functional or UX), its severity, what Autopilot expected and what it saw, and its steps to reproduce.

✅ Whether a scenario covers the over-65 rule, and whether it was completed.

Discuss: would you add a finding to your test cases, report it as a defect, or ignore it? Exploration finds things nobody wrote a test case for. Your test cases prove the rules you agreed on. You need both.

Go further – turn a finding into a test case

Pick one finding from the report. Create a manual test case for it on Submit Loan Request, using the finding's steps to reproduce as your steps, and the requirement's rule as the expected result.

See Running Autonomous Exploration and Reviewing Autonomous Exploration results.

Check it

✅ All three runs of Submit Over-65 Request (yours, Delegate's and the robot's, or the trainer's robot run) are Failed at the age decision, with evidence.

✅ Your comparison table is filled in.

✅ You can name one step wording that would confuse an agent, and you've rewritten it.

docs.title: Nice work!
docs.text:
You judged AI evidence as a tester would: three testers, one verdict, one UiBank defect. Next, you see how the same test case becomes an automation that runs in seconds.

Next → 6. Automate with Studio Web

docs.title: 6. Automate with Studio Web
docs.text:
Leads: All QA · Tools: Trainer demo Studio Web Test Manager

Trainer: create the automated test Trainer: build and check it Trainer: publish it You: link 3 test cases You: check Package Name

Why it matters for you: an automated test gives the same answer every time and costs no AI to repeat. It is how your manual checks become a regression set that runs every night, without anyone clicking through UiBank.

Your trainer turns a manual test case into an automated test in Studio Web and publishes it. Then you link three of your test cases to the trainer's automated tests, so a robot can run them in step 7.

docs.title: Watch: from test case to automated test
docs.text:
Trainer demo Studio Web

You watch this part, about 15 minutes. You don't need to build automations yourself: in most teams, an automation colleague does it. What matters is that you know what happens to your test case, and what the robot checks.

Studio Web is UiPath's browser-based design tool. A Tests project in Studio Web holds automated tests, each linked to a test case in Test Manager. Your trainer built four of them in the project UiBank.BusinessTests:

Automated test What it checks Result today Submit Standard Loan Request A 34-year-old asking for $50,000 is approved ("Congrats…") Passes Submit Underage Request A 17-year-old is rejected ("Sorry…") Passes Submit Over-65 Request A 66-year-old is rejected ("Sorry…") Fails – UiBank approves the loan Submit High-Volume Request A spare the trainer keeps in reserve Fails

docs.title: 1 – Create the automated test
docs.text:
1. In Test Manager, the trainer opens a test case with no automation yet, for example Submit Short-Term Request, and goes to its Automation tab. It says No automation has been assigned to this test case. and offers two buttons: Select Automation (link a test that already exists – you do this below) and Automate in Studio Web (create a new one, Test Cloud only).

  2. The trainer selects Automate in Studio Web. In the panel, they type a new Project name to create the Tests project, pick or create the Test case, and select Add automation. Test Manager confirms with Automation updated successfully!

  3. The Automation tab now shows Studio Link Information and an Open in Studio Web button, which opens the test in a new browser tab.

docs.title: 2 – Build and check it
docs.text:
In Studio Web, an automated test is a short list of steps, called activities, that read much like your manual steps:

✅ Use Browser – open UiBank's loan form in Chrome

✅ Type Into and Select Item – fill in email, amount, term, income and age

✅ Click – submit the application

✅ Get Text – read the result heading UiBank shows

✅ Verify – compare it with the expected result, for example "contains Sorry". This is your acceptance criterion, turned into a check the robot can make.

The trainer can record the clicks and typing instead of adding each activity by hand, with the Autopilot Recorder: it watches what you do in the browser and writes the activities for you (Autopilot Recorder).

Then the trainer selects Debug to run the test in the cloud:

  • Submit Standard Loan Request passes: the Verify reports that the verification passed.
  • Submit Over-65 Request fails: the Verify expected "Sorry" and UiBank returned "Congrats!". The same defect you found by hand in step 4.

The right-hand panel shows Linked test cases: the Test Manager test case this automated test belongs to.

docs.title: 3 – Publish it
docs.text:
A test can only run on a robot after it is published – packaged and stored where Test Manager and the robots can find it.

  1. The trainer selects Publish. The dialog sets the version (1.0.0 the first time) and the Location.
  2. The default location is not the one Test Manager reads, so the trainer picks Orchestrator Tenant Processes Feed and publishes.
  3. Back in Test Manager, the test case's Automation tab now shows Automation Assigned, with Package Source: Tenant Package Feed.

The result is one package, UiBank.BusinessTests, that holds all four tests. Every learner in the class can link to it. See Automating test cases in Studio Web and Publishing a project.

Think about it: which tests are worth automating?

Automate the checks you repeat every release and whose answer you can state exactly, like the age rules. Keep one-off and judgment checks (does the page look right?) manual, or hand them to Delegate or Run autonomously (Preview).

docs.title: Link your test cases to the automated tests
docs.text:
Test Manager

Now you connect three test cases in your project to the trainer's automated tests with the same names. About 10 minutes.

Before you start

✅ Your project has a test case named exactly Submit Over-65 Request, from 3. Generate Test Cases. If yours has another name, rename it first, as described in step 3.

✅ Submit Standard Loan Request and Submit Underage Request came with the project you imported in step 1.

It's your turn now!

  1. In your project, go to Test Cases and open Submit Standard Loan Request.
  2. Go to the Automation tab and select Select Automation.
  3. In the Select Automation panel, keep Package Source on Tenant Package Feed. The list shows Test Case Name, Package, Source and Last Updated.
  4. Shorten the list. The search box matches test case names only, so type the test case name, for example Standard Loan or Over-65. Typing UiBank.BusinessTests there gives No results. To filter by package instead, open the Package filter, tick UiBank.BusinessTests and select Apply.

  5. Select the row Submit Standard Loan Request whose Package is UiBank.BusinessTests, and select Save.

  6. The message Automation updated successfully! confirms it. The Automation tab now shows Package TestCase Name, Package Name (UiBank.BusinessTests) and Package Source (Tenant Package Feed), with the buttons Unlink and Update Automation.

  7. Repeat steps 1–6 for Submit Underage Request and for Submit Over-65 Request, each time picking the test of the same name.

Pick the right row

✅ Ignore the entry called TestCase. It is an empty default file in the trainer's project, not a test.

✅ Ignore Submit High-Volume Request: it is the trainer's spare.

✅ Ignore packages with other names: they belong to other projects on the shared tenant.

✅ Picked the wrong test? Open the test case's Automation tab, select Update Automation and pick again.

docs.title: Check the Package Name column
docs.text:
Check it

In Test Cases, the Package Name column shows UiBank.BusinessTests for Submit Standard Loan Request, Submit Underage Request and Submit Over-65 Request. Your other test cases stay empty: they remain manual.

Can't see the trainer's package, or Save fails? Tell your trainer: they can link the three test cases for you, so you can carry on with step 7.

Optional: build one yourself (not rehearsed)

Curious how it feels to build a test? Try it after the workshop, or now if you finish early. You need:

✅ An App Test Developer licence – building automated tests is not included with App Tester.

✅ The UiPath Studio Web browser extension, in the same browser as UiBank, and UiPath Assistant signed in on your machine to record or pick screen elements.

Use a spare test case such as Submit Short-Term Request, never the three you just linked. On its Automation tab, select Automate in Studio Web and create a new project with your initials in the name, for example UiBank.Tests.<your initials>: a shared Tests project allows only one editor at a time. Then follow About tests in Studio Web.

docs.title: Nice work!
docs.text:
Three of your test cases are now linked to automated tests. In the next step you group them into a regression set with Autopilot chat and run them on a cloud robot.

Next → 7. Build and Run the Regression Set

docs.title: 7. Build and Run the Regression Set
docs.text:
Leads: QA UAT · Tools: Autopilot chat Test Manager Robot

Read what MCP means Label and build the set in chat Configure the automation Run the set Triage in chat

Why it matters for you: a QA manager can organize and run a release regression without code or clicking through grids, and a UAT tester gets a first opinion on every failure in a minute. You still check both against Execution.

Autopilot chat labels your three linked test cases and builds the release regression set for you. You run the set on a cloud robot, then ask chat to triage the result.

Before you start

✅ Submit Standard Loan Request, Submit Underage Request and Submit Over-65 Request show UiBank.BusinessTests in the Package Name column, from 6. Automate with Studio Web.

✅ Your project is open. Autopilot chat opens from the Autopilot icon (the sparkle, top right), set to Edit mode, as in step 1.

docs.title: What MCP means for you
docs.text:
So far, chat mostly read your project. In this step it changes it for the first time: it adds labels and creates a test set. Read this box before you type.

MCP in plain words

Tools. To read or change anything in Test Manager, chat uses approved actions called tools, such as "add labels" or "create a test set". A set of tools is an MCP server. MCP (Model Context Protocol) is the standard plug that connects an AI assistant to a system like Test Manager. Test Manager comes with its own MCP server, so there is nothing to set up. You can see it under Autopilot → ⚙ Chat settings → MCP Servers → From your organization → Test Manager MCP server.

What you'll see. Before each tool runs, chat shows a card with the tool's name and "via MCP server: testmanager". Today you meet these:

✅ Bulk_add_labels – adds a label to several test cases at once

✅ Create_test_set – creates the test set

✅ Assign_test_cases_to_test_set – puts the test cases in it

✅ Get_test_executions – reads run results, for the triage

You approve each one. In Edit mode, every tool card waits for Accept or Reject – reads included, not only changes. One prompt can mean 3–7 clicks. Read the tool name, then select Accept. Built-in tools such as Autopilot Search and Autopilot Chart run without a card.

What it can't do today. With the standard Test Manager tools, chat can't start, schedule or stop a run, and it can't create Execution Insights. You do those with buttons. An admin can add more tools later.

Cost. Each chat turn uses your AI usage pool. Dedicated buttons, such as Evaluate quality or Generate Report, don't (Autopilot usage pool for testing).

Safety. Chat acts as you, so it can only do what your own Test Manager permissions allow. Every action is recorded in your organization's AI Trust Layer audit log. Agent mode runs tools without asking, and the docs label it experimental: stay in Edit mode, so nothing changes without your OK.

More: About Autopilot chat.

docs.title: Label the test cases and build the set
docs.text:
Autopilot chat

A label is a tag on a test case, such as release-2.4. A test set is a group of test cases that run together. You label first, then let chat build the set from the label.

It's your turn now!

  1. Paste this into Autopilot chat and send it:

    Add the label release-2.4 to these test cases: Submit Standard Loan Request, Submit Underage Request and Submit Over-65 Request.

    Chat may first read the test cases (Get_test_cases), then asks to run Bulk_add_labels. It may also read the labels back (GetAllObjectLabelsByObjectId) once per test case. Select Accept each time – about 2–4 clicks, under a minute. It answers with the three test cases it labelled.

  2. Then paste:

    Create a test set called 'Release 2.4 - Loan regression' and assign all test cases with the label release-2.4.

    Chat first finds the test cases with Autopilot Search (no card), then asks to run Create_test_set and Assign_test_cases_to_test_set – about 2–3 clicks, under a minute. It confirms the set and its three test cases.

  3. Type the set name with a plain hyphen, as shown: later prompts look for it by name.

Check it

✅ Before each change, chat showed the tool name and waited for your Accept.

✅ In Test Sets, Release 2.4 - Loan regression exists. On its Test Cases tab it lists exactly 3 test cases: Submit Standard Loan Request, Submit Underage Request and Submit Over-65 Request.

Chat didn't work? Build the set by hand
  1. In Test Sets, create a test set named Release 2.4 - Loan regression.
  2. On its Test Cases tab, under Static Assignment, select Add Test Cases, tick the three test cases and select Assign.
Static or Dynamic Assignment?

A test set gets its test cases in one of two ways:

✅ Static Assignment – pick test cases one by one. The set always runs exactly these. Chat's assign tool adds them this way.

✅ Dynamic Assignment – add labels. The set includes every test case with at least one of them, also ones you label later.

For a release set, Dynamic Assignment on release-2.4 keeps the set up to date by itself. Today, keep the static set chat built.

See Assigning test cases to test sets.

docs.title: Configure the automation
docs.text:
Test Manager

Tell Test Manager where and on which robot the set runs. You do this once per test set.

  1. Open Test Sets → Release 2.4 - Loan regression → Test Cases tab, and select Configure Automation.
  2. Execution folder shows Default (ATB - Agentic Testing Workshop), the shared folder you set as Default Folder in step 1. Leave it.

  3. Runtime type may be empty or show Cloud - VM Testing. Either way, pick Cloud - Serverless Testing. The panel then says "Serverless executions are limited to 15 minutes." – the set needs about one.

    Why not Cloud - VM Testing?

    Cloud - VM Testing is the shared robot that runs everyone's Run autonomously (Preview) tests from step 4. Your set would wait in its queue. Cloud - Serverless Testing starts fresh cloud robots for each run and doesn't wait behind the Run autonomously queue.

  4. Leave Robot account on Any User/Robot account and Machine template on Any machine template.

  5. Under Automation packages, select Autoselect packages. It adds UiBank.BusinessTests - 1.0.
  6. Select Save. Test Manager confirms with Automation details for testset saved successfully!

Optional: formal sign-off (governance)

Need a signed record of the over-65 result? Test Manager can govern test results so approvers sign them.

Want the result governed from the start? Enable it now, before Execute → Automated: Project Settings → Governance (see 9. Decide Go or No-Go for the settings). Forgot? You can still govern the result afterwards – step 9 shows how.

docs.title: Run the set
docs.text:
Test Manager Robot

With the standard Test Manager tools, chat can't start a run, so you use the button.

  1. On the test set, select Execute ▾ → Automated.

  2. The execution page opens, with the message Started Execution for Release 2.4 - Loan regression. In Execution, the run is listed as Automated - Release 2.4 - Loan regression - followed by the date and a number.

  3. Wait about 45 seconds, plus a short queue if the whole class runs at once. Refresh until the header says Finished.

Check it

✅ The header reads 2 passed / 1 failed / 0 not executed (0 none).

✅ Submit Standard Loan Request and Submit Underage Request passed. Submit Over-65 Request failed.

✅ Open the failed Submit Over-65 Request result. Its log shows a failed verification: the test expected UiBank's rejection ("Sorry…") and UiBank answered "Congrats!". That is an assertion – UiBank gave the wrong answer – not a robot error.

Failed is not always UiBank's fault

A robot problem also shows as Failed. If the log says something like Failed to start browser, or all three failed, it's the robot, not UiBank: tell your trainer. See Troubleshooting.

If you or your trainer look at Orchestrator → Jobs, the over-65 job shows as Faulted. That is how Orchestrator reports a failed assertion – it isn't a robot error either.

docs.title: Triage the results in chat
docs.text:
Autopilot chat

A failed test doesn't always mean a broken app: the test itself can expect the wrong result. You made this call by hand in step 4. Now ask chat to check the failure against the requirement.

It's your turn now!

  1. Paste into Autopilot chat:

    For the latest execution of Release 2.4 - Loan regression: give me the totals passed, failed and none. For each failed test case, compare its test data and expected result with the acceptance criteria of the Submit Loan Request requirement. Say whether UiBank breaks the requirement (UiBank defect) or the test expects the wrong result (test defect), and quote the criterion.

  2. Accept each tool card: chat reads the test set, the requirement, the execution, the failed log and the test steps. About 5 clicks, 1–2 minutes.

  3. Compare its answer with Execution. Chat can miscount, so the page is the truth.

Check it

✅ Chat's totals match Execution: 2 passed, 1 failed, 0 none.

✅ Chat calls Submit Over-65 Request a UiBank defect and quotes the over-65 criterion: applicants over 65 are rejected with "Not approved due to age." UiBank approved a 66-year-old, so the test is right and UiBank is wrong. Your own test case's steps may use another age over 65: the verdict is the same.

✅ The success rate is passed out of passed + failed: 2 / (2 + 1) = 66.7%. You decide go or no-go in step 9 – on the defect, not on this number.

Chat calls it a test defect? Ask it to check the test case against the over-65 criterion again, and tell your trainer.

Chat may add a "possible secondary issue": the automation checks for "Sorry", while the criterion says "Not approved due to age." That's a fair point to discuss with the class. It doesn't change the verdict: UiBank approved an applicant it must reject.

Optional: a second opinion with Autopilot Search

Ask chat:

Find all failed test case logs in the latest execution of Release 2.4 - Loan regression.

It uses Autopilot Search (no tool card) and should list Submit Over-65 Request only. Compare the list with Execution. See Search Test Manager project.

Prefer Delegate?

Delegate can triage the same run from your desktop. Replace <PROJECT_PREFIX> with your project's prefix, then paste in your Delegate session:

Summarize and triage the latest execution of the test set Release 2.4 - Loan regression in my Test Manager project <PROJECT_PREFIX>. Don't start a new run. Give me the totals: passed, failed and none. For each failed test case, compare its input data and expected outcome with the acceptance criteria of the Submit Loan Request requirement. Classify it as a UiBank defect (the app breaks the requirement) or a test defect (the test expects the wrong result), and quote the criterion you used.

Approve each request when Delegate asks.

Optional: schedule the set (QA)

A regression set earns its keep when it runs every night or every morning before work. Schedules start automated runs only, never autonomous ones.

  1. On the test set, select Execute ▾ → Create Schedule.
  2. Fill in Schedule (a name, for example Release 2.4 - weekday morning). Test Sets is already filled in.
  3. Pick a Schedule Type:
    • Recurrence → set Repeat to Daily (the default is Hourly), or
    • Advanced → paste the cron expression 0 0 6 ? * MON-FRI (06:00, Monday to Friday).
  4. Set Start Date to tomorrow with the calendar icon (you can't type in the field), set the time to 06:00, and check the Time zone (the default is UTC). A start time earlier than now gives "Start time must be later than the current time". Select Save.
  5. De-activate it right away, so it doesn't run every day after the workshop: go to Execution → Schedules. Your schedule shows Active and its next run. Open its ⋮ menu, select De-activate, then Confirm in the Change active status of test set schedule dialog. The schedule now shows Inactive.

See Creating schedules and Deactivating schedules.

docs.title: Nice work!
docs.text:
Chat labelled your test cases and built the release set, a cloud robot ran it in under a minute, and you know the one failure is UiBank's. Next, turn the results into reports.

Next → 8. Read the Results

docs.title: 8. Read the Results
docs.text:
Leads: QA · Tools: Test Manager Autopilot chat

Read the Dashboard Check the requirement Ask Autopilot chat for charts Generate the Execution Insights report Download the execution PDF

Why it matters for you: a release manager doesn't read test logs. They want coverage, a trend and a short list of what broke. This step turns today's runs into that evidence, and saves the execution PDF you'll attach in step 9.

You ran the over-65 test case three ways and the regression set once. Now read the results the way a QA (Quality Assurance) manager does: first the big picture, then the requirement, then the failures.

docs.title: Read the Dashboard
docs.text:
1. In your project, open Dashboard.

  2. Look at Results Overview. You can switch between Daily and Weekly, nothing else.

    Where is the imported history?

    The 17 executions you imported in step 1 are about 3 years old, and the Dashboard only shows recent weeks. It has no custom date range, so the imported results never appear. The chart starts with today's runs: your manual run, the Delegate run, the autonomous run and the regression set.

  3. Read the two tiles:

    ✅ TOTAL COVERAGE – the share of requirements that have at least one test case. Your project has one requirement with test cases, so it shows 100%.

    ✅ AUTOMATION RATE – how many of your test cases are automated and how many are manual. Only the 3 you linked in step 6 are automated, so most of the project is still manual – for example "70% only manual | 30% automated".

100% coverage doesn't mean ready

TOTAL COVERAGE counts test cases that exist, not test cases that passed. Your requirement is 100% covered, yet one of its acceptance criteria fails. Never report coverage as readiness.

For your admin: more reporting

Two things you won't see today. The Open Defects tile appears only when the project is connected to a defect tracker such as Jira. Trend dashboards across projects need the Insights service. See Dashboard reports.

docs.title: Check the requirement
docs.text:
A release is approved requirement by requirement, so look at the results from that angle too.

  1. Open Requirements → Submit Loan Request.
  2. Open the Test Cases tab. These are the test cases that prove this requirement.
  3. Find Submit Over-65 Request. It belongs here, because it tests the over-65 acceptance criterion.

Submit Over-65 Request isn't in the list?

Then the requirement doesn't know about its failure, and neither do the charts and reports below. On the requirement page, select Assign test case, and add Submit Over-65 Request.

docs.title: Ask Autopilot chat for charts
docs.text:
Autopilot chat can draw a chart or a table from your project in a few seconds. Open your project, click Autopilot (the sparkle icon, top right) and keep the mode on Edit.

It's your turn now!

Send these three prompts, one at a time. Wait for each answer before you send the next one.

  1. Coverage chart

    How many requirements are fully, partially, or not tested?

    Chat uses its Autopilot Chart tool: a pie chart and a table – Fully tested 0, Partially tested 1, Not tested 0. Your one requirement, Submit Loan Request, is Partially tested: the test cases you generated in step 3 are linked, but most haven't run yet. It's a built-in tool, so there's nothing to approve, and it takes under a minute. Read what chat adds under the chart: "tested" means the linked test cases ran, not that every scenario is covered.

  2. Failures by requirement

    Show a chart of failed test cases grouped by requirement.

    Keep the word chart in the prompt. Without it, chat searches and gives you a list instead. Chat draws a bar chart and a table with the count of failed test cases per requirement: Submit Loan Request with 1 failed test case. There's nothing to approve. The chart doesn't name the test case: click the suggestion under the answer, Show the failed test case for your requirement key, to see that it's Submit Over-65 Request.

  3. Your regression set as a table

    List the test cases in Release 2.4 - Loan regression in a table with their labels and their result in the latest execution of that set.

    Chat reads the test set, the test cases, the execution, the logs and the labels of each test case, so in Edit mode you select Accept about 7 times. It takes about 1–2 minutes. You should get 3 rows, each with the label release-2.4: Submit Standard Loan Request and Submit Underage Request Passed, Submit Over-65 Request Failed, and a summary: 2 passed, 1 failed, 0 not run.

Check the AI's numbers

Chat can miscount. Before you put a number in front of a release manager, compare it with Execution. The footer of the chat says it too: "Autopilot can make mistakes. Please double check the responses."

docs.title: Generate the Execution Insights report
docs.text:
Execution Insights is an Autopilot report on why tests fail: the top failing tests, common errors and recommendations. You start it with a button, not in chat. With the standard tools, chat can't create this report, and a dedicated Autopilot button doesn't use your AI usage pool (Autopilot usage pool for testing).

  1. Open Execution → Functional.
  2. Tick the checkbox of your regression execution, Automated - Release 2.4 - Loan regression - …

  3. Select Generate Report ▾ → From selection.

    No row ticked? From last day works too: it picks up everything you ran today. Don't use the longer periods to reach the imported history – it's too old to be included.

  4. You see "Report generation is in progress", and the page switches to the Reports tab by itself, with the status Processing. The report is usually ready in under a minute. No report after 2–3 minutes? Ask your trainer for the reference Insights report and carry on.

  5. Open the report and read its sections: Overview, Top Failing Tests, Common Errors, Error Patterns and Recommendations.

    Under Common Errors you should read something like "The application for an applicant over 65 was accepted instead of rejected…".

  6. Select the download icon (tooltip Download). You get a .docx file with a long, random-looking name. Rename it, for example UiBank-Execution-Insights.docx, and share it with the developers – it's triage input, not release evidence.

Insights is for triage, not for the release decision

The report explains failure patterns. It doesn't tell you whether to ship. Its Recommendations are written for developers (unit tests, logging, and so on): pass them on, but don't treat them as your verdict. See Test result analysis.

docs.title: Download the execution PDF
docs.text:
The execution PDF is the plain, factual record of the run: no AI, just results. It's the evidence you attach to a sign-off.

  1. In Execution → Functional, open your regression execution, Automated - Release 2.4 - Loan regression - …

  2. On the execution page, select the download icon → Download Pdf.

    Use the icon on the execution page. The icon on the Execution list exports every execution to Excel.

  3. Save the file (<PREFIX>-TestResults-<date>_<time>.pdf, with your project prefix) next to your Insights report.

Open it and check:

✅ Summary: 2 Passed / 1 Failed / 0 None

✅ Assertions – Submit Over-65 Request failed its check: UiBank showed "Congrats!" where the test expected "Sorry"

✅ Requirements – Submit Loan Request with its test cases and their results

docs.title: Check it
docs.text:
Check it

✅ Chat's failures chart shows 1 failed test case under Submit Loan Request, and the suggestion names it: Submit Over-65 Request.

✅ The Execution Insights .docx and the execution PDF are saved on your computer.

✅ You can explain in one sentence why 100% coverage doesn't mean ready, and why Execution Insights is triage, not a release summary.

Think about it

Which of today's numbers would you show a release manager, and which would you keep for the test team? Which one could mislead them if you showed it alone?

docs.title: Nice work!
docs.text:
You read the results from three angles – Dashboard, requirement and failures – checked the AI's numbers, and saved the evidence for the decision.

Next → 9. Decide Go or No-Go

docs.title: 9. Decide Go or No-Go
docs.text:
Leads: QA with UAT for the defect draft · Tools: Delegate Autopilot chat Test Manager

Pick your path: Delegate or browser Write the one-page decision Check the decision Optional: defect, routine, sign-off

Why it matters for you: the tools give you evidence, but the call is yours. This step turns today's evidence into a decision a release manager can act on – and defend afterwards.

It's release night, and the release manager wants to know: can we ship the new loan form?

Check these first

✅ Your Release 2.4 - Loan regression run from 7. Build and Run the Regression Set finished with 2 passed / 1 failed / 0 none, and chat triaged the failure as a UiBank defect.

✅ The execution PDF from 8. Read the Results is saved on your computer.

docs.title: Pick your path
docs.text:
Both paths reach the same decision:

  • Path A – Delegate. Delegate repeats the over-65 application in the browser, takes screenshots, and writes a PDF report on your Desktop. Pick it if Delegate is connected on your laptop.
  • Path B – Browser only. Autopilot chat writes the go/no-go summary, and you attach the execution PDF from step 8. Pick it if you don't have Delegate, or if Path A gets stuck.

Got time? Do both, and compare the two reports.

docs.title: Path A – Delegate reproduces the defect
docs.text:
This path uses Delegate, the desktop agent: it works in your browser with your mouse and keyboard. A go/no-go call needs evidence, so Delegate repeats the over-65 application on UiBank, captures the result and puts it in the report.

It's your turn now!

  1. Copy the totals and the triage Autopilot chat gave you in step 7.

  2. Go back to your Delegate session. Replace <PROJECT_PREFIX> with your project prefix from step 1. Paste the prompt below and, in the same message, paste the totals and triage under it:

    Reproduce the UiBank defect in the browser: open https://uibank.uipath.com, apply for a loan with the data from the Submit Over-65 Request test case in my Test Manager project <PROJECT_PREFIX>, and take a screenshot of the result. Then look up its loan ID on the Loan Lookup page, and take a screenshot. Then create a release manager report in PDF for the latest execution of Release 2.4 - Loan regression, and save it on my Desktop. Cover this execution only, not earlier ones. I need a go/no-go recommendation before tonight's sign-off meeting. Base it on UiBank defects only, and list test defects as follow-ups. Include the triage, and add both screenshots and the loan ID as evidence. Under each screenshot, add one line on what it proves against the requirement.

    It takes about 6 minutes.

  3. Approve when Delegate asks. Don't use your browser while it reproduces the defect.

  4. If Delegate asks where to save the report, choose your Desktop. Keep the default file name, and select Submit.

On a Mac, this uses Delegate for macOS (Preview). If it doesn't work, switch to Path B.

Delegate gives the path to the saved report and summarizes it in the chat. Always review its output before sharing. The report shows:

✅ Scope – the execution it covers

✅ Totals – passed, failed and none (the same numbers as the Execution page)

✅ Success rate – passed out of passed + failed

✅ Triage – each failure, whether it's a UiBank or a test defect, and the criterion it breaks

✅ Evidence – the approval and Loan Lookup screenshots, each with what it proves, and the loan ID

✅ Recommendation – GO or NO-GO, and why

Delegate may also list gaps in the requirement or other observations as follow-ups. Check its reasoning against the requirement before you pass them on. UiBank's Loan Lookup page always shows the email someone@sample.com. That's how the demo app works, not a defect to report.

Saved as .md instead of PDF?

Ask Delegate:

Create a PDF of the report and save it on my Desktop.

docs.title: Path B – Autopilot chat writes the summary
docs.text:
This path needs only your browser. Open your project, click Autopilot (the sparkle icon, top right) and keep the mode on Edit.

It's your turn now!

  1. Send:

    Write a go/no-go summary of the latest execution of Release 2.4 - Loan regression for a release manager: scope, totals, success rate as passed out of passed plus failed, each failure with the acceptance criterion it breaks, and a GO or NO-GO recommendation based on UiBank defects only.

  2. Chat only reads your project for this: it uses Test Manager tools such as Get_test_executions and Get_test_case_logs_by_test_execution. These are the same MCP tools you met in step 7 – this time read-only. In Edit mode you select Accept for each one – about 4–6 times. It takes about 1–2 minutes.

What you should get

✅ NO-GO, because one UiBank acceptance criterion fails: a real application defect, not a flaky test or an environment problem.

✅ Totals 2 passed / 1 failed / 0 none, and a success rate of 66.7% (2 out of 2 + 1).

✅ The over-65 criterion quoted from the requirement: applicants over 65 must be rejected.

✅ A release condition: fix the over-65 rule, then re-run the set and get 3 out of 3.

✅ Chat may add a Coverage caveat: only 3 test cases cover the requirement. Keep it in your decision as a note.

Chat recommends GO? Ask it to check Submit Over-65 Request against the over-65 criterion again. Chat can be wrong: the decision is yours.

Then write the one-page decision below, and attach the execution PDF from step 8 as the evidence.

docs.title: Write the one-page decision
docs.text:
A release manager wants one page. Copy the template into an email or a document and fill it in from your report (Path A) or the chat summary (Path B).

GO / NO-GO DECISION – UiBank loan form, release 2.4

Decision:          [GO or NO-GO]
Date and author:   [today's date, your role]

Scope:             [test set and execution name, what it covers]
Totals:            [passed / failed / none]
Success rate:      [passed out of passed + failed, as a %]

Blocking defect:   [what UiBank does wrong, in one sentence]
Criterion broken:  [the acceptance criterion, quoted from the requirement]

Evidence:          [execution PDF file name; screenshots or Delegate report, if any]
Test defects:      [failures caused by the test itself, as follow-ups – or "none"]
Notes:             [caveats, for example limited coverage – or "none"]

Conditions to reach GO:
  1. [what must be fixed]
  2. [what must be re-run, and the result you need]
What a filled-in one looks like 
GO / NO-GO DECISION – UiBank loan form, release 2.4

Decision:          NO-GO
Date and author:   workshop day, QA manager

Scope:             Release 2.4 - Loan regression, latest automated execution
                   (standard, underage and over-65 loan applications)
Totals:            2 passed / 1 failed / 0 none
Success rate:      66.7% (2 out of 3)

Blocking defect:   UiBank approves a loan for an applicant aged 66
                   ("Congrats! You've been approved...").
Criterion broken:  Applicants over 65 must be rejected
                   ("Not approved due to age.").

Evidence:          execution PDF from step 8; the same failure in the manual,
                   Delegate and autonomous runs of step 4
Test defects:      none
Notes:             only 3 test cases in the regression set cover the requirement

Conditions to reach GO:
  1. UiBank rejects applicants over 65.
  2. Release 2.4 - Loan regression re-run: 3 out of 3 passed.

docs.title: Check the decision
docs.text:
Check it

The right call is NO-GO, because UiBank breaks the over-65 rule – not because of the 66.7% success rate.

A success rate of 95% with the same failure would still be NO-GO. A success rate of 66.7% caused only by test defects could be a GO. The rate tells you how much failed; the requirement tells you whether it matters.

Think about it

How did you tell a UiBank defect from a test defect? Would the success rate alone have told you to stop the release? What does a developer need to fix it? How long would all of this take you by hand?

docs.title: Optional extras
docs.text:
Pick what fits your role. None of these is needed to finish the workshop.

Optional: Draft the defect (UAT)

In Delegate, in the same session as Path A:

Draft a defect for the UiBank age defect: title, steps to reproduce, test data, expected and actual result, loan ID, and the screenshots. Save it on my Desktop.

No Delegate? Ask Autopilot chat for the same draft, without the screenshots and the loan ID, and copy the text from its answer.

In a real project, log the defect before the go/no-go call: in your defect tracker, or from the failed result in Test Manager if it's linked to your ALM (Application Lifecycle Management) tool. See Analyzing results.

Optional: Schedule the report as a morning routine (Delegate)

A routine suits a personal report. For the regression run itself, schedule the test set in Test Manager – on the set, Execute → Create Schedule – so it runs on a robot every morning (Scheduling test executions). Let the routine only fetch and summarize the results. Routines are a Delegate feature.

Save it as a routine. Ask Delegate, for example: "Save the report part of this task as a routine called UiBank Release Report. Include my Test Manager project in the routine, so it works when it runs on a schedule." The routine appears under Routines in Delegate's left panel.

Put it on a schedule. Under Scheduled routines, a Day / Week / Month calendar shows every routine with a time slot. New routines wait in the Not scheduled list below it. Drop one onto a time slot or set it to recur, for example weekdays at 8:00 AM.

Start from a ready-made routine. The Test Cloud plugin includes Summarize last night's execution of a test set, already waiting in the Not scheduled list. It returns results only after the test set has run overnight, so on workshop day it finds nothing. To try the same summary now, ask: "Summarize the latest execution of Release 2.4 - Loan regression in my project."

A scheduled routine runs only if its machine is powered on and signed in at the scheduled time.

Optional: Formal sign-off with governance (QA, Test Cloud only)

Some teams need a signed record of who accepted a test result, and in which role. Test Manager's governance feature adds approvers and signatures to test cases and test results, and the signature appears in the execution PDF. Your company may not need it – skip this box if so.

You own your project, so you can switch governance on yourself:

  1. Project Settings → Governance → Enable governance.
  2. Set Default governance state to Governed, and add yourself under Default approvers: type your first name or the start of your email address. Your full name may find nothing, because the directory can list you differently. Leave Signing order off. Select Save. You see "Governance settings updated successfully."

If you can't add yourself as an approver, or the sign icon doesn't appear on your row, ask your trainer to show the signed result in the Trainer Demo project instead.

Didn't switch governance on before your regression run in step 7? Then its results aren't governed yet – govern the over-65 result now. Switched it on in step 7? The result is already governed: open it (item 1), then skip to item 3.

Before you sign: your name and email appear in the signature

The signature and the PDF show your name and email address, and the signed result stays on the shared workshop tenant. Don't share the signed PDF outside the class, and crop screenshots before you use them. The test case's Latest Results grid shows your email under Executed By too: crop it as well.

  1. Execution → open your regression execution → open the Submit Over-65 Request result.
  2. Turn on the Governed toggle. Approval status shows In work.
  3. Select the pencil next to the status. In Set approval status, select In review. From now on the result is locked: nobody can edit it until it's signed.
  4. Open the Governance tab of the result. On your approver row, select the sign icon. In the Sign test case panel, fill in Your role at time of signature, for example QA Manager, add a comment if you like, and select Sign.
  5. The status changes to Signed, and your approver row shows Signed with your name. Download the execution PDF again: it now has a Governance section with the signature.

In a real project, switch governance on before the run: new results are then governed from the start. Moving a result to In review locks it, so make any override or comment first. See Testing process governance and Governance for test results.

Discuss: when is an override OK?

Test Manager lets you override a result – for example, change a Failed result to Passed – with a mandatory comment. The override is visible on the result, so it works as a documented waiver (Overriding test results).

Discuss with your neighbour, without changing your results:

  • Would you override the over-65 failure to reach GO? (No: UiBank is wrong, and the override would hide a real defect.)
  • When would an override be fair? For example, a failure caused by the test itself, when the app did the right thing and re-running doesn't help.
  • Who in your company should be allowed to override, and who should sign it off?

docs.title: Go further
docs.text:
Stay in the same Delegate or Autopilot chat session – it remembers the run and the report:

✅ "Summarize the failures in three bullet points I can paste into Teams or Slack."

✅ "Add a section to the report with recommended next steps for the developers."

✅ "Rewrite the summary for a developer, with the failed check and the actual value UiBank returned."

More ideas in More Prompts to Try.

docs.title: Nice work!
docs.text:
You turned today's runs into a documented NO-GO: a UiBank defect against a named acceptance criterion, with evidence, and a clear condition for GO.

Next → You did it!

docs.title: You did it!
docs.text: Congratulations! You took UiBank's new loan form from a requirement to a documented release decision – without writing a line of code.

docs.title: What you did today
docs.text:
BA You made a vague requirement measurable and turned it into test cases, including the over-65 case that caught the defect.

UAT You ran the same test case yourself, with Delegate and with a robot, and saw all three stop at the same UiBank defect.

QA You built and ran a regression set with Autopilot chat, read the results without being fooled by 100% coverage, and called NO-GO on a broken acceptance criterion, not on a success rate.

docs.title: Which helper for which job
docs.text:
Helper Use it to Good to know Autopilot buttons in Test Manager Evaluate a requirement, generate test cases, create the Execution Insights report Dedicated buttons don't use your AI usage pool Autopilot chat in Test Manager Ask about your project, label test cases, build test sets, triage failures, draw charts, write a go/no-go summary In Edit mode it asks before each action. With the standard tools it can't start runs or create Execution Insights. Each prompt uses your AI usage pool Delegate on your desktop Run a manual test case on UiBank, reproduce a defect with screenshots, write a PDF report Works with your mouse and keyboard. Each task uses your AI usage pool Robots Run a test case autonomously (Preview), run the automated regression set on Cloud - Serverless Testing Started from Test Manager, no code. Runs use your organization's robot capacity Studio Web Turn a test case into an automated test (your trainer showed it) You reused the trainer's tests with Select Automation

Costs and limits are explained in Autopilot usage pool for testing.

Remember

The helpers do the legwork. You decide what to test, which failures matter, and whether to ship.

Next → Troubleshooting & Next Steps

docs.title: Troubleshooting & Next Steps
docs.text:
You took one UiBank requirement all the way to a release decision. This section helps you get unstuck and take the same way of working back to your team.

You used three helpers today: Autopilot in Test Manager (the buttons and the chat), Delegate on your desktop, and robots that the trainer provided (Run autonomously and the serverless regression run). See Introduction for the full picture.

docs.text:

docs.title: Taking this to your team
docs.text:
✅ Test Cloud only: Autopilot chat and its charts, the Test Manager MCP tools, Execute Manually without a test set, Automate in Studio Web, governance (formal sign-off), the PDF report of a single test result, Find obsolete tests and the autonomous features (Run autonomously and Autonomous Exploration, both Preview) need Test Manager on Test Cloud. On the Flex licensing model, chat, charts, Find obsolete tests and autonomous testing aren't available. Before you plan a rollout, check what your tenant has in the Test Manager feature availability table.

✅ Usage pool and licences: every Autopilot chat turn and every Delegate task uses your monthly AI and Agentic usage pool. The dedicated Autopilot buttons (Evaluate quality, Generate tests, Import Test Cases, Generate Report) don't. Run autonomously uses the tenant's App Test Platform Units instead. How big your allowance is depends on your user licence and your organization's plan. When the pool is spent, chat and Delegate pause until an admin grants a top-up or the month resets – there's no automatic fallback. See Autopilot usage pool for testing.

✅ Edit mode as the safe default: in Autopilot chat, Edit mode shows each tool and waits for your Accept or Reject. Agent mode runs the tools without asking, and the docs label it experimental. Start every new prompt in Edit mode, and keep Agent mode for prompts you've already checked in Edit mode.

✅ Delegate approval modes: Cautious asks before every operation, Adaptive runs read-only actions on its own and asks before anything that writes, changes or runs something, Full access never asks. In regulated teams, admins set the approval mode, allowed tools, blocked apps and sites, and models centrally in Automation Ops policies, and can lock them so users can't change them. See Delegate centralized configuration and Delegate security settings.

✅ Secrets: logins for the application under test belong in Orchestrator Credential assets, never in prompts, test steps or test data.

✅ Regular runs: schedule a regression test set in Test Manager (test set → Execute → Create Schedule). Schedules start automated runs only, not autonomous ones.

For admins: give Autopilot chat more tools

Today you used the tools that ship with Test Manager. With those standard tools, chat can't start, schedule or stop a run, or create Execution Insights – you used the buttons for that. An admin can add more tools:

  • the Performance Testing MCP server, so chat can analyze performance runs
  • MCP servers built in Orchestrator (MCP Servers → Add MCP Server) that expose your own automations or APIs, for example a process that creates test data or test accounts in another application. Some server types, such as the Platform and Swagger MCP servers, are in Preview

Users then see them in Autopilot chat → ⚙ Chat settings → MCP Servers, under From your organization. The Automation Ops Autopilot policy controls which tools, MCP servers and models chat may use. See About Autopilot chat and About MCP servers.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:
✅ Insights dashboards: with Insights enabled, the ready-made Test Manager Execution Report dashboard tracks results across projects and over time. See Test Manager Execution Report.

✅ Jira or Azure DevOps: connect your project to your defect tracker, then Create Defect from a failed test case log, and the Dashboard's Open Defects number fills in. See Defect synchronization and Connecting an Azure DevOps project.

✅ Performance and accessibility testing: Test Manager can reuse automated tests to check how an application behaves under load, and to report accessibility issues. Both build on automations that your automation colleagues create. See Performance testing overview and Accessibility testing.
